artist: Chris Forsyth & the Solar Motel Band
label: Paradise of Bachelors
description: A four-part instrumental suite that traces the electric guitar's evolution from Jerry Garcia-style lead lines through Sonic Youth noise, Solar Motel is Forsyth's move from solo-guitar Primitivism into full-band, jam-length rock. It's less a set of songs than a single continuous guitar exploration.
lineage: Forsyth's crossover from the American Primitive solo-guitar world into full-band Dead- and Television-indebted jamming, launching the Solar Motel Band.

artist: Chris Forsyth & the Solar Motel Band
label: No Quarter
description: The Solar Motel Band's breakthrough tightens Forsyth's guitar suites into denser, riff-driven pieces, still stretching well past the length of a normal rock song. It made year-end lists across outlets that don't usually cover instrumental guitar-jam records.
lineage: Follow-up to Solar Motel that cemented Forsyth's reputation as a leading voice in Philadelphia's Dead-adjacent guitar-jam underground.

album: Flash Forward to the Good Times
label: Kemado Records
description: The former Beachwood Sparks/Jonathan Wilson-band multi-instrumentalist's solo debut is loose, sun-baked country-psych, heavy on pedal steel and warm analog fuzz. It sounds like an extension of the same Laurel Canyon-revival scene he helped build as a sideman.
lineage: A solo outlet for a musician central to both Beachwood Sparks and Jonathan Wilson's band, tying together several strands of the 2000s LA cosmic-country revival.
key_tracks: Flash Forward to the Good Times

label: Sub Pop
description: Beachwood Sparks' debut revived Gram Parsons-style cosmic country rock for the Sub Pop indie audience, all pedal steel, close harmonies and gently psychedelic guitar. It landed a few years before the mid-2000s revival it anticipated.
lineage: An early, direct descendant of Gram Parsons and the Flying Burrito Brothers that predates and helped set up the 2000s-2010s cosmic-country revival scene.

label: Sub Pop
description: A more ornate, string-and-organ-dressed follow-up to the debut, Once We Were Trees leans further into orchestrated psychedelic country than straightforward twang. It's the fullest expression of the band's early Laurel Canyon revivalism.
lineage: Deepens Beachwood Sparks' Gram Parsons/Byrds-descended sound with fuller studio arrangements, a direct ancestor of the mid-2000s cosmic-country revival.

label: Sub Pop
description: A reunion album made squarely within the 2010s cosmic-country revival scene they'd predicted a decade earlier, The Tarnished Gold sounds warmer and more relaxed than the debut without losing its pedal-steel-heavy Parsons worship. It plays like a welcome-home record for a band whose sound had finally caught up with everyone else.
lineage: Beachwood Sparks re-entering the cosmic-country conversation just as bands like Woods and Kevin Morby were carrying the same Gram Parsons/Dead lineage forward.

label: Sub Pop
description: Athens punks turned Dead-worshipping jammers, Arbor Labor Union's Sub Pop debut is fuzzed-out, repetitive guitar rock that treats a single riff as a launchpad for extended noise. It's the loudest, most distortion-caked branch of the cosmic-country revival covered here.
lineage: Formed from Georgia's hardcore/punk scene before turning toward Dead- and Meat Puppets-style jamming, embodying the album's title, per Terry's coverage, of 'transcendental twang.'

label: Sub Pop
description: A brighter, more classic-rock-structured record than I Hear You, New Petal Instants sounds like the Traveling Wilburys reimagined by Meat Puppets and Wilco, with cleaner hooks under the still-present fuzz. It's the band easing off pure noise toward actual songcraft.
lineage: Shows Arbor Labor Union moving from distortion-first jamming toward more structured, Dead/Wilburys-style country rock.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: With a new lineup, Yonder is Arbor Labor Union's most introspective, nocturnal record, cleaner and more inward than the kaleidoscopic New Petal Instants but no less indebted to the Allmans and Neil Young. Josh Terry called it the best thing he'd heard in January 2023.
lineage: A quieter turn within Arbor Labor Union's catalog that still reaches for the same Dead/Allman Brothers well as their earlier fuzzed-out records.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: A short follow-up EP to Yonder that keeps the same winding, left-field guitar grooves and Dead-indebted chord changes in a tighter package. Terry named it among his favorite 2025 releases for its crunchy, unpredictable playing.
lineage: A compact continuation of Arbor Labor Union's post-Yonder sound, still working the same Dead/Allman Brothers vein.

label: New West Records
description: Color Green's second album is a meditation on grief and clarity delivered through loose, live-feeling jams, from the devastating hush of '5:08' to the sprawling 'Kick the Bucket.' Four vocalists and two guitarists trade lines the way a band that treats every gig as improvisation would.
lineage: Follows the quartet's Aquarium Drunkard-released debut with a jump to New West, still working the same '60s SoCal folk-rock and Dead/Allmans-descended jam vocabulary.

label: Self-released
description: Wilder Maker frontman Gabriel Birnbaum's solo album mines character studies of quiet desperation over lush, psychedelic-tinged folk-rock, closer to Paul Simon's narrative songcraft than his main band's more experimental side. It's a mature, unhurried record built on empathetic detail.
lineage: A solo outlet for the Wilder Maker frontman that leans further into plainspoken, character-driven folk-rock storytelling.

label: Congrats Records
description: Cohen's fourth album, made with partner and producer Sam Evian at their Catskills studio Flying Cloud, is a hazy collage of memory built from years of home recording. Guest turns from Sufjan Stevens and Clairo sit inside a soft-focus, folk-pop sound that favors atmosphere over hooks.
lineage: Grows out of the Flying Cloud/Sam Evian Catskills recording circle, part of the same upstate-New York scene as several other C6 and C5 field-guide artists.

label: Night Bloom Records
description: A gentle, warmly-produced set of songs about distance and homecoming, Year Away favors soft-focus folk-pop arrangements over the twangier end of the C6 sound, closer to a hushed Laurel Canyon lullaby than a jam band.
lineage: Part of the same overlapping West Coast singer-songwriter circle as Anna St. Louis and Jess Williamson, who both guest on each other's records.

label: House Band (self-released)
description: A debut LP from a loose LA supergroup with ties to Bedouine, Midnight Sister and Spoon, Aventurine spreads twelve tracks over nearly an hour of sprawling, heady grooves that recall electric-era Miles Davis as much as the Dead. Terry called it more Can than country, but its jam-length instrumental patience puts it squarely in this lineage.
lineage: An LA session-musician side project extending the cosmic-jam end of the scene into krautrock and fusion territory.

label: Earth Libraries
description: Andrews' fifth album as the Yawns is a tranquil, piano-and-guitar record written in Red Hook, Brooklyn, with Luke Temple guesting on guitar and bass. It's quieter and more contemplative than his earlier full-band records, closer to Little Wings' loose, handmade songwriting.
lineage: The latest entry in Andrews' long-running Woodsist/Earth Libraries-adjacent solo project, drawing explicitly on Little Wings' DIY songwriting.

label: Rhino Entertainment
description: Formed by the late Neal Casal to soundtrack a Grateful Dead box set before becoming its own band, this self-titled third LP pushes the instrumental jam group toward a groovier, cosmic-disco direction. It's an all-instrumental record that wears its Dead pedigree (bassist Dan Horne also plays in Beachwood Sparks) openly.
lineage: Descends directly from the Grateful Dead's own jam vocabulary, connected to the wider LA cosmic-country scene through shared musicians like Dan Horne.

label: New West Records
description: A full-band collaboration with New Zealand's Marlon Williams, Plastic Bouquet brightens Kacy & Clayton's usual spare Canadian prairie folk into warmer, harmony-heavy country rock. Williams and Kacy Anderson's voices trade and blend across a set of plainspoken duets.
lineage: A one-off widening of Kacy & Clayton's traditional-leaning catalog through collaboration with Marlon Williams, closer to breezy country rock than their usual austere folk.

label: Woodsist / Mare
description: St. Louis's second album opens up her stark debut into brighter, more orchestral arrangements, recorded with Woods' Jarvis Taveniere and featuring Jess Williamson, Kacey Johansing and Oliver Hill among the guests. It trades the gritty apparitions of her first record for patient, present-tense contentment.
lineage: Connects directly to the Woodsist label and the overlapping West Coast singer-songwriter circle of Jess Williamson and Kacey Johansing, who both appear on the record.

label: Dead Oceans
description: A deliberately harder-to-parse record than Walker's earlier Fahey-descended solo-guitar albums, Deafman Glance buries anti-folk songwriting under synths, warped studio effects and Chicago free-improv contributors like Cooper Crain and Nate Lepine. Walker has called it a record for 'coming up or coming down.'
lineage: Walker's most experimental studio record, pulling his American Primitive guitar roots into Chicago's free-improv and noise scene.

label: Self-released
description: New Jersey's Garcia Peoples keep working the same dual-guitar-jam vein as their earlier records here, all extended solos and interlocking leads named directly for Jerry Garcia's playing. It's dense, riff-forward psych-jam rock built for headphones or a long drive.
lineage: Part of the Woodsist-adjacent New Jersey/New York jam underground alongside Endless Boogie, taking their name and sound directly from Garcia's guitar style.

label: Birdman Records
description: Howlin Rain's debut is a cult favorite of thick, fuzzed-out Crazy Horse-style guitar rock, Ethan Miller's voice straining over extended riffing that owes as much to the Allman Brothers as to Neil Young. It set up the heavier, more maximalist sound Miller would carry through the American Recordings years.
lineage: Ethan Miller's move from the noisier Comets on Fire into a more classic-rock, Crazy Horse/Allman Brothers-descended sound, launching his long-running Howlin Rain project.
key_tracks: Dancers at the End of Time

label: Fire Records
description: Davis's debut draws on pristine Laurel Canyon songwriting from the '60s and '70s and dresses it in gentle country phrasing, all warm harmonies and unhurried tempos. It reads as a straight continuation of the soft-rock/country-rock lineage this lane traces back to.
lineage: A newer voice working directly in the Laurel Canyon/country-rock tradition that feeds this lane, closer to '70s soft rock than jam-band twang.

label: Arrowhawk Records
description: With Barry Walker Jr. on pedal steel, Silverstein alternates expansive instrumentals with songs sung in a delivery pitched between Bill Callahan's deadpan and Kurt Vile's drift. NPR pegged it as cosmic country in the vein of Beachwood Sparks and Silver Jews.
lineage: Part of the Rose City Band/Arrowhawk Records circle of Pacific Northwest cosmic-country instrumentalists.

label: Perpetual Doom
description: A West Coast lifer and Little Wings collaborator, Baggett makes crunchy, warm Crazy Horse-style rock here, all snaking guitar solos and B3 organ. It sits comfortably alongside the mellower, jam-friendly end of this lane.
lineage: Connected to the Little Wings/Kyle Field circle of West Coast lo-fi songwriters, carrying their loose sensibility into fuzzier guitar-rock territory.

label: Self-released
description: Sam Owens' debut as Sam Evian is a warm, lightly psychedelic bedroom-folk record, its analog haze pointing toward the Flying Cloud studio he'd later build with Hannah Cohen. It's an older record Terry has singled out in show recaps as a formative favorite.
lineage: The starting point for the Flying Cloud/Hannah Cohen upstate-New York recording circle Evian would go on to anchor as a producer.

label: Terrible Records
description: Ben Schwab's (Golden Daze, Drugdealer) trio project debuted with this five-song, mostly-covers EP, its title track (an Iain Matthews cover) sung by Sam Burton over spare, warm arrangements. It's a slight but gorgeous record with strong ties to the wider Tompkins Square/West Coast folk circle.
lineage: Connects the Golden Daze/Drugdealer LA psych scene to the softer country-folk world through guest vocalist Sam Burton.

label: Self-released
description: An Auckland quartet's sophomore LP mixes desert twang, brooding psych atmospherics and country phrasing into immersive, dynamically wide-ranging arrangements. Terry described it as swinging between rowdy and delicate across its runtime.
lineage: Part of a small but growing Antipodean cosmic-country scene taking the Dead/Beachwood Sparks lineage outside the US.

label: Self-released
description: A pandemic-written, Dead-inspired set of psychedelic twang with a rotating cast of guest vocalists, Down Home is warmer and more collaborative than the duo's earlier records (one of which was produced by Margo Price). It's a loose, front-porch take on cosmic country.
lineage: Nashville duo working the same Dead-indebted country-rock vein as the city's Coin Collection/Rich Ruth scene, with overlapping guest musicians.

label: Rough Trade Records
description: Ballgame's full-length debut sets warm, '70s-inflected songwriting inside commanding, theatrical vocal performances and tasteful, non-pastiche arrangements. It leans closer to Laurel Canyon soft-rock revivalism than jam-band twang, but fits the same '70s-revival umbrella.
lineage: A newer entry in the '70s soft-rock/country-rock revival that runs alongside this lane's jammier, Dead-descended wing.

label: Self-released
description: Recorded at Chicago's Thawed Out festival in 2025, this live document catches Sam Cantor's band stretching their warm, Dead-adjacent country-rock songs out on stage. Terry has named Minor Moon among his favorite Chicago bands.
lineage: A live snapshot of Chicago's own small cosmic-country scene, adjacent to acts like Ryley Walker in the city's guitar-forward underground.
key_tracks: I Could See It Coming (Live at Thawed Out)

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Formed from the ashes of Smith Westerns, Whitney's debut pairs Julien Ehrlich's high falsetto with warm horn charts and loose, country-tinged guitar picking, closer to the Band's easy soulfulness than to jam-band sprawl. It became a defining record of mid-2010s soft, horn-driven indie rock.
lineage: Grew out of the collapse of Smith Westerns' glammy power-pop into a gentler, horn-and-pedal-steel-inflected country-soul sound.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Whitney's most ambitious record, grown from acoustic demos into full arrangements with Brad Cook and John Congleton at Sonic Ranch, folds synths into their usual horn-and-guitar warmth. It's a left-field stretch for the band without losing the easy melodicism of the debut.
lineage: Whitney's furthest reach from their country-soul debut, though still built on the same warm, horn-inflected songwriting core.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Terry called this Whitney's best-sounding, most confident record, a return to fuller, more assured songwriting after SPARK's detour into synths. The horns and falsetto are still the core of the sound, just delivered with more conviction.
lineage: A confident late-career synthesis of Whitney's country-soul debut and their more expansive mid-period records.

label: Tiny Engines
description: Wild Pink's debut is a quiet, synth-tinged indie-rock record already reaching for the widescreen, heartland-adjacent atmosphere John Ross would refine on later albums. It's rougher and more DIY than the band's Royal Mountain-era work.
lineage: The starting point of Wild Pink's catalog, before their sound expanded into the fuller heartland-indie of A Billion Little Lights.

label: Tiny Engines
description: A synth-washed haze of guitar rock drawing openly on Springsteen and the War on Drugs, Yolk in the Fur is where Wild Pink's widescreen, heartland-indebted sound came into focus. It's warmer and more melodic than the debut while keeping its DIY scale.
lineage: Draws directly on Springsteen's heartland rock and the War on Drugs' synth-guitar sound, filtered through a smaller-scale indie band.

label: Royal Mountain Records
description: Wild Pink's breakout record layers pedal steel and strings under John Ross's introspective, plainspoken lyrics, arriving at a lush, heartland-scaled sound. Terry has called it home to some of the finest rock songwriting he's heard from a touring band.
lineage: Wild Pink's fullest realization of pedal-steel-dressed indie rock, sitting at the crossover point between heartland rock and the C1 twang scene.

label: Royal Mountain Records
description: Written and recorded after John Ross's cancer diagnosis, ILYSM is a more inward, cathartic record than its predecessor, its heartland-scale arrangements now carrying real emotional weight. Terry called it an excellent, cathartic listen.
lineage: A personal, health-crisis-driven turn within Wild Pink's pedal-steel-and-synth heartland sound.

label: Fire Talk
description: Recorded mostly live, Wild Pink's fifth album trades some of ILYSM's studio polish for a rougher, heavier rock palette. Terry named it the band's best record, singling out the title track as a fist-raising ode to moving on.
lineage: Wild Pink's rawest, most rock-forward record to date, still carrying the heartland/pedal-steel DNA of their Royal Mountain years.

label: Gulcher Records
description: Vile's debut is a hazy, homespun collection of fingerpicked drones and mumbled melodies recorded largely alone on a four-track. It set the template for his sleepy-eyed guitar style before Matador ever came calling. It's for listeners who want the slacker-rock revival at its most unpolished origin point.
lineage: Grew out of the War on Drugs' Philadelphia scene and the lo-fi Bandcamp/cassette underground; its haze fed directly into the countrygaze and slacker records of the 2010s.

album: God Is Saying This to You...
label: Mexican Summer
description: A compilation of early home-recorded tracks that bridges Constant Hitmaker and his Matador debut, showing the same murmured vocals and unhurried acoustic-electric picking before a full band thickened his sound. It's a stopgap for completists tracing his rise from bedroom tapes to indie stardom.
lineage: Part of the same lo-fi Philadelphia tape underground that produced Constant Hitmaker; a bridge into the more full-band Matador era.

label: Matador Records
description: Vile's Matador debut adds full-band muscle and squalling guitar solos to his stoned drawl, making it the loudest and most rock and roll record of his catalog. Songs like the motorik-driven opener show him leaning into Crazy Horse-style fuzz for the first time. It's the record where the War on Drugs alum became a solo guitar hero in his own right.
lineage: Signing to Matador connected Vile's Philly lo-fi scene to the wider indie-rock world, setting up the 2010s slacker and jangle revival that followed him.

label: Matador Records
description: A quieter, more assured record than its predecessor, built on fingerpicked acoustic figures and Vile's half-asleep drawl, this is often cited as his creative breakthrough. It slows the tempos down and lets the songwriting carry the weight rather than the guitar pyrotechnics. It's the album that turned casual fans into believers ahead of his commercial peak.
lineage: Refines the Crazy Horse-and-folk hybrid of Childish Prodigy into the more meditative style that would define his Wakin on a Pretty Daze and B'lieve I'm Goin Down eras.

label: Matador Records
description: A sprawling, patient record full of long, meandering songs that stretch his laconic style to its most spacious extreme, including several tracks that pass the nine-minute mark. It trades the tighter pop songwriting of Lotta Sea Lice for hypnotic, repetition-based jams. It's for fans who want to sink into Vile's world for a while rather than get a quick hit.
lineage: Extends the loose, hypnotic guitar-drone side of his songwriting that traces back through Crazy Horse to his own Smoke Ring for My Halo.

label: Verve Records
description: Vile's first album after leaving Matador for Verve leans further into home-studio synth textures and drum-machine pulses while keeping his familiar mumbled melodies intact. It's looser and more playful than his 2010s work, closer to a solo bedroom record again. It's for longtime fans curious how his sound evolved once he started producing almost everything himself.
lineage: A return to the DIY, self-produced instincts of his earliest lo-fi tapes, now filtered through two decades of studio experience.

label: Matador Records
description: A loose, conversational set of duets and trade-off songs between two of indie rock's most deadpan drawlers, built on unhurried fingerpicked guitar interplay. The two swap verses and harmonize in a way that feels like eavesdropping on old friends. It's for anyone who wants Vile's haze and Barnett's wit in the same room.
lineage: A direct collaboration linking the American slacker-guitar lineage (Vile) with the Australian deadpan-songwriter tradition (Barnett), each feeding the other's fanbase.

label: Self-released
description: One of Alex Giannascoli's earliest self-released Bandcamp full-lengths, recorded on GarageBand with warped, pitch-shifted vocals and drum-machine loops. It's rougher and stranger than the records that made him famous but already shows his knack for a warped melodic hook. It's for the deep-catalog listener who wants to hear Alex G before the songcraft got polished.
lineage: Part of the early-2010s Bandcamp lo-fi boom that would later be called out by Frank Ocean's use of his music, feeding directly into DSU and the rest of his catalog.

label: Self-released
description: Another early self-recorded Bandcamp album from Alex G's prolific 2011 run, built from warbling home-studio pop songs and pitched vocal manipulation. The songwriting is skeletal and the fidelity is intentionally rough, but melodic hooks poke through the murk. It's for listeners tracing the earliest roots of his songwriting before Domino signed him.
lineage: Continues the same DIY GarageBand aesthetic as Winner, part of the flood of Bandcamp full-lengths that built his cult following before DSU broke through.

label: Self-released
description: A collection of short, murky home recordings that lean further into the pitched-vocal manipulation and tape-hiss atmosphere that became his early trademark. Songs blur together into a woozy, half-remembered whole rather than standing as individual singles. It's a transitional record for fans tracking his path toward DSU's breakout.
lineage: Sits in the same self-released Bandcamp run as Winner and Race, the DIY foundation that eventually caught Orchid Tapes' and then Domino's attention.

label: Self-released
description: The last of Alex G's run of purely self-released Bandcamp full-lengths before signing to Orchid Tapes, still built on lo-fi four-track pop songs with warped, childlike vocals. Melodically it's a bit more confident than Rules, hinting at the songwriting leap DSU would make. It's for listeners who want the full arc of his self-taught bedroom period.
lineage: Closes out the self-released Bandcamp era that set up his signing to Orchid Tapes for DSU and eventually Domino Recording Co.

label: Orchid Tapes
description: Alex G's breakthrough, a warm and melodic leap from his earlier tapes that caught the attention of Frank Ocean and Orchid Tapes alike, mixing pitch-shifted vocals with genuinely gorgeous pop songwriting. It's still lo-fi but far more melodically assured than his self-released run. It's the record most people point to as his arrival as a songwriter to watch.
lineage: The culmination of his self-released Bandcamp period, and the record that plugged him into the Orchid Tapes/bedroom-pop scene before Domino signed him.

label: Domino Recording Co.
description: Alex G's Domino debut pushes his warped pop songs into stranger, more processed territory, with pitch-bent vocals sitting alongside skeletal drum machines and unsettling interludes. It's a deliberately harder listen than DSU, trading immediacy for atmosphere. It's for fans who like the unease under his prettiest melodies.
lineage: First release for Domino after his Bandcamp/Orchid Tapes run, expanding his cult audience while keeping the same bedroom-pop DNA.

label: Domino Recording Co.
description: A genre-hopping record that swings from fiddle-laced country pastiche to noisy skronk to gentle folk within its short, restless tracklist. It's Alex G at his most eclectic, refusing to settle into one style for more than a couple of minutes at a time. It's for listeners who want the fullest picture of his range.
lineage: Broadens the bedroom-pop template of Beach Music with country and folk textures that anticipate his later, more song-oriented Domino albums.

label: Domino Recording Co.
description: A woozy, unsettling record that folds pitch-shifted vocals, folk fingerpicking, and eerie electronic textures into some of his most emotionally direct songwriting, written partly about addiction and loss close to him. Josh Terry has called it the album that soundtracked his memory of 2019. It's often cited as the most cohesive statement in Alex G's catalog.
lineage: Builds on the genre-collage approach of Rocket while tightening the emotional focus, setting up the more expansive God Save the Animals.

label: Matador Records
description: Will Toledo's Matador debut re-records and remasters highlights from his sprawling self-released Bandcamp catalog, bringing his hyper-verbal, deadpan songwriting to a wider audience for the first time. It's noisier and more chaotic than his later full-band records. It's for fans curious how his bedroom-era songs sounded once given an actual budget.
lineage: Bridges Toledo's twelve self-released Bandcamp albums with the full-band Matador era that produced Teens of Denial and beyond.
key_tracks: Bad Role Models, Good I Am

label: Matador Records
description: A full-band re-recording of Toledo's beloved 2011 Bandcamp double album, keeping the original's confessional, wordy songwriting about a doomed teenage relationship while giving it a much bigger, more anthemic sound. Both versions are essential; this is the one most fans discovered first. Note: the original 2011 self-released Twin Fantasy is the same songs in rawer, lo-fi form and is worth hearing alongside it.
lineage: A direct remake of Toledo's own Bandcamp-era masterpiece, connecting his DIY lo-fi songwriting roots to his mature full-band sound.

label: Matador Records
description: A deliberately polarizing pivot toward synths, drum machines, and even EDM-adjacent production, released partly under the alter-ego alias Trait, while keeping Toledo's anxious, funny-sad lyricism intact. It traded the noisy guitar rock of Teens of Denial for something colder and more electronic. It's for fans willing to follow the band away from its jangle-rock comfort zone.
lineage: A deliberate break from the Crazy Horse and jangle-rock guitar sound of Teens of Denial, showing the DIY-to-major-indie pipeline can still take creative risks.

label: Matador Records
description: A concept album set at a fictional university, this record returns Car Seat Headrest to a bigger, more guitar-driven full-band sound after the electronic detour of Making a Door Less Open. Toledo's wordy, theatrical songwriting is at its most ambitious here, built around a cast of recurring characters. It's for longtime fans who wanted the band's rock muscle back.
lineage: A return to the anthemic guitar-rock lineage of Teens of Denial after the band's synth-pop experiment, keeping Toledo's literary songwriting intact.

album: The Double EP: A Sea of Split Peas
label: Marathon Artists
description: A compilation pairing Barnett's first two self-released EPs, introducing her rambling, deadpan talk-singing and wry observational lyrics to an international audience for the first time. The guitar tone is loose and unpolished, closer to garage rock than the more produced records that followed. It's the release that put her on critics' radars before her proper debut LP.
lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY scene and Barnett's own Milk! Records; set the stage for the deadpan Australian songwriter wave that followed, including Fred Thomas-style funny-sad storytelling in the US.

album: Tell Me How You Really Feel
label: Milk!/Mom+Pop
description: A heavier, more direct record than her debut, with fuzzed-out guitars backing pointed lyrics about self-doubt, sexism, and anger. The production is thicker and the tempos slower, giving her deadpan delivery more room to sting. It's for listeners who want Barnett's wit turned toward something angrier.
lineage: Follows directly from Sometimes I Sit and Think..., sharpening the same slacker-guitar and deadpan-lyric approach into more overtly political territory.

label: We Are Busy Bodies
description: The Welsh duo's debut album packs deceptively simple garage-pop melodies into a scrappy, ramshackle energy, with the pair's back-and-forth deadpan vocals doing most of the heavy lifting. Songs whip by quickly, favoring hooks over polish. It's the record that set up their prolific run before Sub Pop signed them.
lineage: Part of the UK DIY garage-pop underground that runs parallel to the American slacker/jangle revival, later connecting the band to Sub Pop and the wider Bandcamp scene.
key_tracks: We Don't Need Room For Lovin'

label: Sub Pop Records
description: The Bug Club's second Sub Pop record streamlines their oddball garage-pop into catchier, tighter songs, with the jokes landing harder and the choruses stickier than ever. The dual vocals of Sam Willmett and Tilly Harris trade lines with an easy chemistry throughout. It's for listeners who want slacker-pop songwriting that's actually secretly very well-crafted.
lineage: Continues the band's garage-punk-to-power-pop evolution begun on Green Dream in F#, now filtered through a major indie label's reach.

label: Self-released
description: Will Anderson's debut full-length as Hotline TNT buries plainspoken pop melodies under thick sheets of guitar fuzz and noise, setting up the countrygaze-adjacent wall-of-sound style he'd refine on Cartwheel. It's rawer and murkier than the later records but already has the hooks. It's for fans who want the noisiest end of the jangle/shoegaze crossover.
lineage: Kicks off Hotline TNT's run from DIY noise-pop toward the more country-tinged, festival-ready sound of Cartwheel and Raspberry Moon.

label: Carpark Records
description: Ducks Ltd.'s debut full-length sets the duo's template of chiming, propulsive guitar interplay over drum-machine-assisted rhythms, drawing on '80s college-rock jangle filtered through a modern anxious lyric sheet. Tom McGreevy's plainspoken vocals ride on top of Evan Lewis's careening guitar lines. It's for fans of Sarah Records-style jangle brought into the present.
lineage: Draws on the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle-pop lineage and the Toronto DIY scene; set up Harm's Way's fuller studio sound.

label: Carpark Records
description: Recorded in Chicago with producer Dave Vettraino and featuring guests from Lawn, Ratboys, and Dehd, this is Ducks Ltd.'s most fleshed-out record, precise and propulsive jangle-pop with careening riffs and power-pop melodies. Josh Terry wrote the album's press bio and calls it one of the year's best indie rock records. It's the fullest realization yet of the duo's college-rock-meets-anxiety songwriting.
lineage: Builds on Modern Fiction's jangle foundation with a bigger, more collaborative studio sound tying Toronto and Chicago's indie-pop scenes together.

label: Salinas Records
description: Bonny Doon's debut is a gentle, unhurried collection of plainspoken country-folk songs built on loping tempos and warm, conversational vocal harmonies between Bill Lennox and Bobby Colombo. It's understated where their later records get looser and more rock-facing. It's for fans of hushed, front-porch songwriting.
lineage: Grows out of Detroit's indie scene (with ties to Waxahatchee, whose Saint Cloud the band would later back); sets up the more Woodsist-style slacker sound of Longwave.

label: Woodsist
description: A warm, sleepy-eyed sophomore record that became a slow-burn cult favorite, pairing loose, unpolished guitar interplay with plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and drift. Its patient tempos and conversational vocals put it squarely in the Woodsist label's slacker lineage. It's for fans who want comfort-food indie rock that never raises its voice.
lineage: Continues the band's hushed country-folk sound on the classic slacker label Woodsist, connecting them to the broader 2010s Kurt Vile/Real Estate axis.

label: Sub Pop Records
description: A dreamier, more polished turn for the garage-glam lifer Kyle Thomas, trading his usual fuzzed-out riffs for jangly, synth-dusted power pop with a wide-eyed, sun-drenched feel. It's a gentler record than his 2010s output but keeps his knack for an instant hook. It's for fans who like their power pop with a cosmic-country glow.
lineage: King Tuff's catalog runs from 2000s garage-punk through Sub Pop glam-rock; Smalltown Stardust pulls him into the same jangly, twang-adjacent revival as his 2010s peers.

label: Buzz Records
description: Casper Skulls' debut EP introduces the Toronto band's dual-vocal, college-rock-indebted guitar pop, drawing on Pavement and R.E.M.-style jangle with conversational, story-driven lyrics. It's shorter and scrappier than their later full-lengths but sets the band's voice from the start. It's for fans who want the earliest version of their sound.
lineage: Part of Toronto's Buzz Records jangle-pop roster alongside acts like Weaves; a direct forerunner to Mercy Works and Knows No Kindness.

label: Buzz Records
description: Casper Skulls' full-length debut expands their college-radio jangle into bigger, more anthemic arrangements while keeping the dual-vocal chemistry between Melanie St-Pierre and Neil Bednis at the center. The lyrics lean into storytelling and small-scale drama over ringing, layered guitars. It's for fans of R.E.M.-descended Canadian indie rock.
lineage: Follows directly from Lips & Skull on Buzz Records, continuing Toronto's jangle-pop lineage into a fuller studio sound.

label: Buzz Records
description: A more confident, dynamically varied record than their debut, still anchored by ringing guitar interplay and dual-vocal storytelling but pushing into denser arrangements and darker lyrical territory. It's the sound of a band settling comfortably into its own identity within Toronto's jangle-pop scene. It's for fans who followed the band from their Buzz Records beginnings.
lineage: The most developed entry in Casper Skulls' Buzz Records run, later followed by Kit-Cat on Next Door Records.

label: Next Door Records
description: Casper Skulls' latest LP has the dual-vocal chemistry and college-radio jangle of a band drawing on Pavement, R.E.M., and Superchunk, described by Josh Terry as full of lived-in warmth. Guitars ring and interlock while the vocal trade-offs keep the songs feeling conversational. It's for longtime fans of the band's steady evolution.
lineage: Continues the jangle-pop lineage established on Buzz Records, now on Next Door Records with a warmer, more assured sound.

label: You've Changed Records
description: Written in response to ghostly samples McKiel found on a used reel-to-reel tape, this record blends hushed, fingerpicked songwriting with warped found-sound textures into something inventive and haunting. It's a quieter, more experimental turn than straightforward jangle-pop but keeps a strong melodic core. It's for fans of Canadian DIY songwriting with a spectral edge.
lineage: Part of the You've Changed Records roster connecting Maritime Canada's indie scene to the wider lo-fi/jangle underground; feeds into Hex's continued collaboration with Jay Crocker.

label: You've Changed Records
description: A second collaboration with producer Jay Crocker, this record folds more synths and studio texture into McKiel's hushed songwriting without losing the strange, homemade intimacy of Bobby Joe Hope. It's a favorite of Josh Terry's that he never got around to writing about on release. It's for fans of understated, atmosphere-first Canadian indie rock.
lineage: Continues the Crocker/McKiel partnership begun on Bobby Joe Hope, part of the same You've Changed Records lineage.

label: Trouble in Mind Records
description: A shambling, K Records-worthy set of hooky, unhurried indie pop from this Melbourne trio, all ringing guitars and plainspoken vocals over loping tempos. It's cheap, cheerful, and unfussy in a way that recalls the DIY jangle-pop of decades past. It's for fans of Flying Nun-descended guitar pop with an Australian slacker drawl.
lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY jangle-pop scene that also produced Dick Diver and Terry, distributed internationally by the American slacker-rock label Trouble in Mind.

label: Chapter Music
description: Recorded at a beach house on Phillip Island, this second Dick Diver LP is loose, warm, and conversational, built on ringing guitars and half-sung, half-spoken vocals in the vein of the Go-Betweens and the Clean. It's a defining record of the early-2010s Melbourne jangle-pop revival. It's for fans who want the sound that inspired a wave of Australian slacker-pop bands.
lineage: Grew out of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene alongside Boomgates and Twerps; directly influenced Chook Race and the broader countrygaze/jangle revival abroad.

label: Mom + Pop
description: Lili Trifilio's breakout EP pairs bright, hooky power-pop guitars with plainspoken lyrics about body image and self-doubt, catching viral attention that pushed Beach Bunny from bedroom project to touring band. The songs are short, direct, and instantly catchy. It's for fans of Chicago's guitar-pop scene at its most immediate.
lineage: Grows out of Chicago's DIY guitar-pop scene alongside acts like Dehd; connects 2010s bedroom-pop songwriting to a more festival-scale power-pop sound on Blame Game.

label: Ever/Never Records
description: This New York quartet's self-titled debut is a hooky, jangly and twangy power-pop rock record with blistering riffs and meaty choruses, released by the fast-rising Ever/Never label. It's punchy and immediate, favoring rock and roll swagger over polish. It's for fans who want the twang-adjacent side of the current power-pop wave.
lineage: Signed to Ever/Never, the same New York label behind Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band and National Photo Committee, tying the band into the current DIY jangle/twang underground.

label: Third Man Records
description: Produced by Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever's Joe White, this sophomore LP from Melbourne's the Belair Lip Bombs is frenetic, interlocking power pop fronted by the commanding Maisie Everett. The guitars careen and lock together in a way that recalls Australia's jangle-rock lineage while the choruses aim straight for arenas. It's among the strongest straight power-pop records of its year.
lineage: Connects Melbourne's jangle-rock scene (via producer Joe White of Rolling Blackouts C.F.) to Third Man Records' wider power-pop and garage-rock roster.
key_tracks: Don't Let Them Tell You (It's Fair)

label: Angel Tapes
description: This trio's debut full-length tightens the raucous energy of their 2024 EP into hook-forward, dynamic indie rock, packing frantic energy and earworm melodies into a lean 25 minutes. Delicate falsetto verses give way to explosive, unrelenting choruses across the tracklist. It's for fans who want their power pop with real teeth.
lineage: Released via Fire Talk's Angel Tapes imprint, connecting the band to the current New York DIY guitar-pop underground alongside labelmates in the same scene.

label: Psychic Hotline
description: Mountain Man's Alexandra Sauser-Monnig's sophomore solo record is her most playful, writing kinetic, off-kilter pop songs that evoke Talking Heads, Finom, and Sheryl Crow rather than straight folk. Her lyrics stay conversational and perceptive even as the arrangements get bouncier. It's for fans who want folk-rooted songwriting that takes unexpected pop turns.
lineage: Grows out of the Mountain Man/Big Thief-adjacent folk circle, pushing outward into twangy indie pop territory that overlaps with the jangle revival.

label: Self-released
description: Cult New York duo Frog's sixth album is folky, lo-fi and scrappy, described by Stereogum's Chris Deville as though Modest Mouse made a Pinegrove album. Highlights include the piano-led opener and a banjo-anchored lead single, with aching lyrics wrapped in charmingly unadorned production. It's for fans who want deadpan, funny-sad songwriting without any studio gloss.
lineage: Frog has been active since 2012 in New York's DIY scene, connecting Drag City-style funny-sad songwriting to the jangle/lo-fi Bandcamp underground.

label: Bar/None Records
description: Blue Broderick's Diners project goes full power-pop on this impeccably written, breezy guitar-pop record produced by Mo Troper, with clear DNA from Tom Petty, Big Star, and Fountains of Wayne. There's no filler across the ten tracks, each one built for maximum hum-along appeal. It's for fans who want classic power-pop songcraft filtered through a bedroom-pop sensibility.
lineage: Connects Broderick's earlier lo-fi Diners records to the wider Bandcamp power-pop revival via producer Mo Troper, a key figure in that scene.

label: Self-released
description: This Columbus power trio's three-song EP is pummeling, loud, and varied, with each track sounding markedly different but united by an animated heaviness, per Josh Terry, who calls the band the future of indie rock. Fronted by a husband-and-wife duo plus a drummer, it's a live-wire document of a genuinely ferocious band. It's for fans of noisy Midwestern guitar rock that hits hard in short bursts.
lineage: Part of the current Midwest DIY noise-rock underground that overlaps with the slacker/jangle scene at its loudest, rowdiest edge.

label: Self-released
description: Joe Glass's debut showcases his knack for an airtight hook across a dozen slightly twangy, ramshackle rockers pulling from Nuggets-style garage pop and '90s indie rock. Josh Terry has said it would have been a newsletter favorite had he heard it upon release. It's the record that predates his work alongside bandmate Kai Slater in Sharp Pins.
lineage: Part of the Chicago/Rockford DIY power-pop underground surrounding Lifeguard and Sharp Pins, feeding into Glass's later, more polished Snakewards.

label: Self-released
description: Chicago songwriter Ben Astrachan's solo debut is maximalist and ambitious, packing each of its 13 tracks with wailing guitars and a multitude of '60s-and-'70s-indebted melodic twists. It's conceptual rock music delivered in an off-kilter, deliriously infectious way rather than as straight pastiche. It's for fans of Chicago's current crop of ebullient, detail-obsessed guitar-pop songwriters.
lineage: Emerges from the same Chicago scene as Smushie and Shoulderbird, connecting classic-rock revivalism to the current power-pop/jangle underground.

label: Self-released
description: A self-released Wisconsin power-pop record with effortless hooks and a '90s rock sensibility, continuing Graham Hunt's steady run of home-recorded guitar-pop albums. The songwriting is direct and unfussy, favoring melody over studio polish. It's for fans who want deep-catalog power pop from outside the usual coastal scenes.
lineage: Sits between If You Knew Would You Believe It? and Timeless World Forever in Hunt's self-released discography.

label: Self-released
description: Another entry in Graham Hunt's prolific self-released catalog, continuing his blend of hooky, home-recorded power pop with wide-ranging classic-rock and psych touches. It appeared on Josh Terry's 2025 longlist among the year's most worthwhile guitar-pop records. It's for listeners tracking his steady, low-key discography.
lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing solo catalog that runs directly into American Pyramid's bigger studio sound.

label: Self-released
description: Hunt's sixth full-length is his most maximalist yet, recorded at Minnesota's Pachyderm Studios after years of home recording, with frantic late-'90s pop-rock hooks, autotuned detours, and euphoric grooves recalling Screamadelica. Josh Terry calls it cutting-edge while somehow still sounding instantly familiar. It's the fullest studio treatment his songwriting has gotten to date.
lineage: The culmination of Hunt's self-released catalog, moving from bedroom recording to a proper studio while keeping the same playful, hook-heavy songwriting.
key_tracks: Waiting for You to Come Home

label: Keeled Scales
description: This Brooklyn band's debut, originally formed in North Carolina, eschews the twang-and-shoegaze sound of their home-state peers for something more its own: brutal, pounding riffs paired with dual lead vocals and patiently pastoral arrangement shifts. Released by the Texas label Keeled Scales, it stands apart from the countrygaze pack while sharing its scene. It's for fans who want the loudest, least twangy corner of the current DIY guitar-rock underground.
lineage: Formed within North Carolina's twang-and-shoegaze scene before relocating to Brooklyn, giving it ties to both C4 countrygaze and straighter jangle/power-pop rock.

label: Disaster Records
description: Bill Callahan's debut as Smog, self-released on the tiny Disaster Records before Drag City took over his catalog, is the rawest, most primitive document in the discography: four-track hiss, barely-there arrangements, and a flat, untrained voice that would only get drier from here. It has none of the later records' craft, but it is the ground floor the whole Drag City deadpan sound was built on. A curiosity for completists more than an entry point.
lineage: The earliest Smog release, predating Callahan's move to Drag City proper; its bedroom-tape austerity set the low bar of fidelity that Julius Caesar and Wild Love would build outward from.
key_tracks: I Want to Tell You About a Man

label: Drag City
description: Callahan's first release on Drag City proper is a long, sprawling collection of four-track sketches, twenty-two songs deep, sung in the same flat monotone that would define the project. It is looser and more song-count-heavy than the more focused records that followed, closer to a demo tape than a finished album. A deep cut for listeners tracing the earliest Drag City catalog.
lineage: Callahan's first Drag City release, part of the same early-1990s Chicago catalog as Silver Jews' first records, establishing the label relationship that carried through the rest of his career.

label: Drag City
description: A six-song EP released between Julius Caesar and Wild Love, Burning Kingdom keeps the same close-mic'd, unhurried delivery as the albums around it, with songs about failed relationships sung in Callahan's flattest register. It is a minor but characteristic release, mostly of interest once a listener already knows the full-lengths on either side of it.
lineage: Sits between Julius Caesar and Wild Love in the early Smog catalog, part of the same Drag City run that established Callahan's deadpan template.

label: Drag City
description: A four-song EP released the same year as The Doctor Came at Dawn, Kicking a Couple Around is a small, stark release in the same hushed vein as that album, co-released in the UK by Domino. It is a minor but consistent entry, four more songs of flat, unhurried dread from the same period as one of Callahan's bleakest full-lengths.
lineage: Released alongside The Doctor Came at Dawn, part of the same mid-1990s stretch of Smog's catalog and Drag City's growing UK partnership with Domino.

label: Drag City
description: A dub-remix companion to Dream River, released a year later, this record strips Callahan's own vocals almost entirely out of the mix in favor of instrumental versions, echo and reverb treatments applied to the same groove-based arrangements. It is a curio rather than a proper follow-up, more interesting to fans of the source album's rhythm section than to newcomers. A deep-catalog oddity that shows how far Callahan was willing to reframe his own material.
lineage: A dub reworking of Dream River's grooves, made with the same Austin-era band, extending that record's loose, rhythm-forward direction into an almost entirely instrumental register.

label: Drag City
description: Oldham's twenty-first studio album as Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, recorded at his own home in Louisville, mixes devastating lines with real humor delivered in his familiar half-spoken drawl. No Expectations' Josh Terry named it an essential, haunting entry and a good doorway into Oldham's three-decade catalog for a new listener. It sits comfortably alongside the catalog's other late-period highlights for its mix of plainspoken sadness and wit.
lineage: A recent continuation of the Bonnie 'Prince' Billy catalog begun on I See a Darkness, recorded and self-produced at home the way much of the early Palace material was.

label: Drag City
description: An early Silver Jews 7-inch EP, recorded before Starlite Walker and credited to Berman alongside Pavement's Bob Nastanovich and a guitarist billed as Hazel Figurine, this is even more ramshackle and hiss-laden than the debut LP that followed. Five brief, half-sketched songs capture Berman's deadpan phrasing before it had settled into the band's fuller sound. A collector's item more than a way in.
lineage: One of Silver Jews' earliest Drag City releases, predating Starlite Walker and documenting the band's shambling origins alongside Pavement's Bob Nastanovich.

label: Drag City
description: Released the year before Starlite Walker, this EP catches Silver Jews mid-transition from scattershot 7-inch singles toward the fuller, more confident songwriting of the first LP. 'Bar Scene from Star Wars' shows the deadpan, pop-culture-referencing humor that would become a Berman trademark already fully formed. A useful stepping stone for listeners who want to trace the band's development before the debut.
lineage: The last Silver Jews EP before Starlite Walker, part of the same early Drag City run that also produced Dime Map of the Reef.

label: Gnomonsong
description: A full collaboration between Hurley and the hushed Brooklyn folk trio Ida, released on the Gnomonsong label Devendra Banhart and Vetiver's Andy Cabic ran to champion older folk eccentrics, this pairs Hurley's wandering drawl with Ida's close, quiet harmonies. It softens his usual talking-blues looseness into something gentler and more arranged than his solo records. A good way into Hurley's later-period work for listeners coming from indie folk rather than old-time music.
lineage: A documented link between Hurley's decades-old deadpan-folk style and the 2000s indie-folk revival, both through Ida's own hushed harmony sound and Gnomonsong's role in reintroducing him to a younger audience.

label: Domino
description: Royal Trux co-founder Neil Hagerty's first outing under his own name, released the same year he produced Bill Callahan's Woke on a Whaleheart, is a loose, riff-driven solo record that keeps the classic-rock damage of Royal Trux's later albums without Jennifer Herrema's co-lead vocals. It is a minor entry mostly of interest to listeners tracing Hagerty's connections to the Drag City deadpan circle through his production work. Not deadpan-country itself, but part of the same label ecosystem.
lineage: Documents Hagerty's solo work in the same period he began producing for Bill Callahan, part of the wider Drag City-adjacent circle even though released on Domino.

label: Drag City
description: Recorded while Baird was still a member of Philadelphia psych-folk band Espers, her solo debut is a hushed, largely solo-voice-and-guitar record of traditional and original ballads, her clear, unadorned alto compared by critics to Sandy Denny and Pentangle's Jacqui McShee. It is one of the plainest, most old-time-adjacent records to come out of the 2000s Philadelphia freak-folk scene. A quiet, patient entry point for listeners who want folk-revival singing without ornamentation.
lineage: Grew out of Baird's time in Espers and the Philadelphia psych-folk scene, carrying Anglo-American folk-ballad singing into the indie-folk revival alongside Gillian Welch and Iron & Wine.

label: Nonesuch
description: Amidon's first Nonesuch album, produced by longtime collaborator Thomas Bartlett, reworks old-time and traditional songs (its title track a Civil War-era ballad) into spare, occasionally jazz-inflected arrangements built around his plain, unhurried voice and banjo. Raised by folk-revival parents and steeped in the Harry Smith Anthology as a teenager, Amidon treats old songs as raw material to be reshaped rather than preserved. A good entry point for listeners who want old-time source material filtered through an experimental indie-folk sensibility.
lineage: Extends the Anthology of American Folk Music tradition into 2010s indie folk, sharing Nonesuch's roster with Gillian Welch and drawing on the same song-collecting impulse behind Jake Xerxes Fussell's records.

label: Signature Sounds
description: Ritter's second album, and first to reach a wider audience, is a plainspoken, largely acoustic set of story-songs steeped in Americana imagery, closer to Woody Guthrie and early Bob Dylan than to the more baroque indie folk of the period. It built his reputation as a literate, road-tested songwriter well before he had any major-label backing. A solid, unpretentious entry point into his catalog.
lineage: An early-2000s example of the plainspoken folk-songwriter revival running parallel to Gillian Welch and Iron & Wine, built on classic American folk and country storytelling forms.

label: V2 Records
description: Ritter's major-label-distributed breakthrough widens his sound with a full band and more overtly political songwriting, most notably on the sprawling 'Thin Blue Flame'. It kept his plainspoken, story-driven core intact while reaching a considerably larger audience than his earlier records. Often cited as his creative peak.
lineage: Builds on the plainspoken storytelling of The Golden Age of Radio with fuller band arrangement, part of the same 2000s singer-songwriter wave as Bon Iver and Iron & Wine's early records.

label: Virgin Records
description: Marling's debut, released when she was 18 and recorded with members of Noah and the Whale, pairs plainspoken, folk-club fingerpicking with a voice far older than her years, earning her a Mercury Prize nomination. Songs like 'Ghosts' and 'Night Terror' show a songwriter already working in a spare, traditional-adjacent idiom distinct from the freak-folk and chamber-pop of her UK peers. A strong entry point into the UK wing of the 2000s indie-folk revival.
lineage: Part of the mid-2000s London nu-folk scene alongside Noah and the Whale and Mumford & Sons, closer in spirit to the American Gillian Welch/Iron & Wine axis than to the festival-folk mainstream that scene later fed.

label: Virgin Records
description: Marling's second album, produced by Ethan Johns, is a more assured and traditionally-minded record than her debut, its title drawn from The Odyssey and its songs built on plain fingerpicked guitar and understated string arrangement. It won the Brit Award for Best British Female and is generally considered her breakthrough into a more mature, folk-revival-steeped songwriting voice. A good second stop after the debut.
lineage: Continues Marling's move away from London nu-folk toward a more classic, Anglo-American folk-revival sound, produced by Ethan Johns in the same lineage as Ryan Adams and Kings of Leon's roots-rock records.

label: Sub Pop
description: Jurado's second Sub Pop album is a hushed, largely acoustic record of quiet, character-driven songs, closer to a whispered short story collection than to the label's rock reputation. It established the plainspoken, melancholy songwriting style he would work in for the next two decades. A key early document of Sub Pop's non-grunge, folk-leaning side.
lineage: An early entry in Sub Pop's quieter, singer-songwriter-driven roster alongside Iron & Wine, part of the same late-1990s turn toward hushed acoustic folk within indie labels historically known for louder music.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Jurado's first album for Secretly Canadian, produced by Richard Swift, pairs his plainspoken, melancholy songwriting with slightly fuller, more layered arrangement than his earlier Sub Pop records. It is a transitional record between his hushed 1990s-2000s catalog and the more psychedelic direction he'd pursue with Swift on later albums. A solid mid-career entry point.
lineage: Marks Jurado's move from Sub Pop to Secretly Canadian and the start of his long production partnership with Richard Swift, which would push his sound in increasingly experimental directions afterward.

label: Secretly Canadian
description: Continuing his partnership with producer Richard Swift, Saint Bartlett keeps Jurado's plainspoken, hushed songwriting at the center while adding subtle vintage-tape warmth and occasional gospel-tinged backing vocals. It is widely regarded as a high point in his 2000s-2010s catalog, balancing intimacy with just enough production color to stand apart from his earlier, sparer records.
lineage: The fullest realization of the Jurado-Swift partnership begun on Caught in the Trees, before Jurado's sound drifted further into psychedelia on Maraqopa and beyond.

label: Partisan Records
description: The debut from this Vermont trio of Amelia Meath, Alexandra Sauser-Monnig and Molly Sarle is almost entirely unaccompanied voice, three-part harmonies stacked over minimal or no guitar, drawing directly on old-time Appalachian singing traditions. It is one of the starkest, most purely vocal records in the whole lane, closer to field-recording austerity than to studio folk-pop. A key document for listeners who want the close-harmony end of the indie-folk revival at its most extreme.
lineage: Rooted directly in old-time Appalachian a cappella and shape-note singing, later a documented influence on Meath's more electronic work in Sylvan Esso, showing how far the folk-revival's vocal tradition could travel.

label: Nonesuch Records
description: Originally self-released before Nonesuch picked it up, the Rhode Island band's second album pairs hushed, hymn-like arrangements (pump organ, musical saw, clarinet) with plainspoken, often historically-minded lyrics, epitomized by the title track's meditation on evolution and faith. It won them Mojo's Breakthrough Artist award and remains their best-known record. A good entry point for the more austere, chamber-folk end of the 2000s revival.
lineage: Part of the same late-2000s wave of hushed, antique-instrumented indie folk as Fleet Foxes and Bon Iver, though rougher and more explicitly rooted in old hymnal and gospel forms.

label: Self-released
description: Justin Vernon's pre-Bon Iver band, formed with childhood friends in Eau Claire before relocating to Raleigh, released this self-titled debut as a plainspoken, full-band roots-folk record, still years from the hushed falsetto he'd develop as a solo artist. It is a minor, self-released document, but a genuine missing link for tracing how Vernon's songwriting grew out of a full band before he stripped it down alone in a cabin. A curiosity for completists of the For Emma lineage.
lineage: The band Justin Vernon led before its breakup sent him back to Wisconsin to record For Emma, Forever Ago alone, making this a direct, documented root of the whole modern hushed-indie-folk singer-songwriter mode.
key_tracks: As Long as I Can Go

label: East Side Digital
description: A Boston band working the same country-punk seam as Uncle Tupelo but a few years ahead of the No Depression name, Corn River pairs Jim Ryan's mandolin and Cheri Knight's harmony vocals over plainspoken, unhurried songs about hard luck and leaving. Trouser Press called the band one of America's least formulaic roots-rock combos, and this debut shows why: it splits the difference between bluegrass instrumentation and indie-rock songcraft without leaning hard on either. An overlooked early document of the scene before it had a name.
lineage: Predates Uncle Tupelo's No Depression by roughly the same moment, part of a loosely connected wave of late-1980s bands (also including the Silos) working out insurgent country independently before the genre had a shared identity.

label: Quarterstick
description: Produced by Butthole Surfers guitarist Paul Leary, the Bad Livers' debut runs bluegrass instrumentation at punk speed and volume, Danny Barnes' banjo and deadpan songwriting anchoring a trio that Rolling Stone praised for its 'virtuoso flash and poignant simplicity'. It sits at the acoustic-punk edge of the insurgent-country moment, closer to thrash-grass than to Uncle Tupelo's Telecaster twang. A key document of Austin's more eccentric contribution to the scene.
lineage: An Austin-scene parallel to the Chicago and Belleville insurgent-country bands, fusing bluegrass virtuosity with the same punk energy that drove cowpunk and the Waco Brothers.

label: Sugar Hill
description: The Bad Livers' first album for Sugar Hill Records tightens the trio's thrash-grass sound into more clearly song-based material, with Sing Out! praising Danny Barnes' 'quirky and inventive' writing and The Washington Post singling out his 'timeless, deadpan voice'. It is the most accessible entry point into a catalog that never quite fit any single genre label. A good pick for listeners who want the bluegrass-adjacent edge of 1990s insurgent country.
lineage: Marks the Bad Livers' move to Sugar Hill, a label with deeper bluegrass-world connections than their earlier home Quarterstick, while keeping the same punk-inflected string-band core.

artist: Kelly Hogan and the Pine Valley Cosmonauts
label: Bloodshot Records
description: Kelly Hogan's second solo record, backed by Jon Langford's rotating Pine Valley Cosmonauts ensemble, leans into warm, classic-country arrangement behind her clear, expressive alto. Hogan had already sung on the Cosmonauts' Bob Wills tribute, and this record cements her as one of Bloodshot's most purely gifted vocalists rather than a songwriter-first act. A good showcase for the label's backing-band ecosystem as much as for Hogan herself.
lineage: Documents the close working relationship between Kelly Hogan and Jon Langford's Pine Valley Cosmonauts, part of the same tightly interconnected Chicago Bloodshot scene as the Waco Brothers and Robbie Fulks.

album: Salute the Majesty of Bob Wills
label: Bloodshot Records
description: Jon Langford's revolving-door Pine Valley Cosmonauts enlist a who's-who of the Bloodshot roster, Neko Case, Alejandro Escovedo, Robbie Fulks and Kelly Hogan among them, for a tribute to Western swing bandleader Bob Wills. It functions as a mission statement for the whole insurgent-country scene's roots reverence, treating a pre-rock country bandleader as a direct ancestor worth genuine celebration rather than ironic quotation. A useful single record for hearing several Bloodshot voices in one place.
lineage: A documented crossroads record for the Chicago insurgent-country scene, gathering Neko Case, Robbie Fulks, Kelly Hogan and Alejandro Escovedo under Jon Langford's direction to honor a shared Western-swing ancestor.

label: Yep Roc
description: Melissa Swingle's Chapel Hill band debuts with a spare, spooky sound steeped in Southern gothic imagery closer to Flannery O'Connor than to barroom twang, its songs of local Chatham County characters given a slide-guitar, minor-key hush. It is a quieter, stranger entry point into the gothic-country wing of 1990s insurgent country than the more famous Handsome Family or 16 Horsepower records, rooted specifically in rural North Carolina rather than Chicago or Denver.
lineage: An early document of the Chapel Hill scene's own gothic-country strand, later moving to Bloodshot for its two most acclaimed records, part of the wider Southern-gothic wing alongside the Handsome Family and 16 Horsepower.

label: Bloodshot Records
description: Trailer Bride's Bloodshot debut deepens the band's spooky, minor-key sound, Melissa Swingle's flat, world-weary drawl carrying songs of sin, death and small-town dread over sparse slide guitar. It ties the band more directly into the Chicago-centered Bloodshot roster while keeping its distinctly North Carolina gothic sensibility intact. A good next step for listeners who start with the band's Yep Roc debut.
lineage: Moves Trailer Bride onto Bloodshot Records, aligning the Chapel Hill gothic-country project with the wider insurgent-country label ecosystem centered in Chicago.

label: Rounder/Philo
description: A Maine-raised, Austin-based songwriter who won the Kerrville Folk Festival's New Folk award before this, his first nationally distributed record, No Angel Knows sets plainspoken, blue-collar character studies against unfussy acoustic and pedal-steel arrangement. It is a quieter, more folk-leaning cousin to the louder Texas insurgent-country bands of the same decade, closer to Guy Clark's storytelling tradition than to cowpunk. A solid way into Cleaves' long Rounder-era catalog.
lineage: Grew out of the same Austin singer-songwriter scene as the Old 97's and the Gourds, though working in a quieter folk-storyteller mode closer to the Texas songwriter tradition than to twangy bar-band rock.

label: Mid-Fi Records
description: Steve Dawson and Diane Christiansen's Chicago band debuts with a self-released, four-track-recorded record that got heavy local radio play and drew major-label interest the band ultimately turned down. Its husband-and-wife co-lead vocals and blend of rock, country and pop mark it as a gentler, more melodic cousin to the punkier Waco Brothers and Bloodshot roster active in the same city at the same moment. A good introduction to Chicago's less rowdy insurgent-country wing.
lineage: Formed from the ashes of the twang-punk band Stump the Host, part of the same mid-1990s Chicago scene as the Waco Brothers and Freakwater, though working in a warmer, duet-driven pop-country idiom.

label: Bloodshot Records
description: Langford's first official solo album looks back at his hometown of Newport, Wales, filtered through the same punk-country hybrid he brought to the Mekons and Waco Brothers. It shows the Welsh-born bandleader's songwriting stripped of a full group identity for the first time, still built on blunt, working-class storytelling and barroom energy. A useful companion to the Waco Brothers catalog for hearing Langford's voice on its own.
lineage: Langford's first record under his own name after founding the Mekons and Waco Brothers, extending his punk-meets-country songwriting into explicitly autobiographical territory.

label: Chunk
description: This Massachusetts band's debut is a hushed, largely acoustic record of plainspoken heartbreak songs, closer in spirit to a barroom last call than to the louder cowpunk bands of the same moment. Joe Pernice's flat, weary voice and the band's unhurried tempos gave the Northeast its own quiet answer to the twangier Midwest and Texas scenes. A key document of New England's contribution to 1990s insurgent country.
lineage: Part of the same small-club Northampton, Massachusetts scene that produced Dinosaur Jr. and the Pixies' extended circle, applying that region's DIY ethic to a hushed, pedal-steel version of insurgent country.

album: Lost Somewhere Between the Earth and My Home
label: Virgin
description: Carla Bozulich's Los Angeles band fuses old-time fiddle and country songforms with noise-rock volume and dissonance, a combination closer to Sonic Youth or the Jesus Lizard than to anything on Bloodshot's roster. Bozulich's voice swings between a plaintive country croon and a full-throated shriek, often within the same song, making this a key document of insurgent country's noisiest, most avant-garde fringe. A challenging but rewarding entry point for listeners who want the genre pushed toward art-punk extremity.
lineage: Extends country and old-time fiddle music into noise-rock territory via Bozulich's earlier band Ethyl Meatplow, a documented outlier within 1990s insurgent country that anticipates later noise-adjacent Americana.

label: Mac's Record Label
description: A wordless, tape-warped song cycle Mac DeMarco pieced together while driving cross-country, all warm Rhodes, brushed drums and looping guitar vamps instead of his usual slack-jawed vocals. It plays like a private travelogue, mixing his usual chorus-pedal haze with lounge and ambient touches. For listeners who want the DeMarco sound stripped of singing.
lineage: Extends the bedroom-pop haze of his Captured Tracks records into instrumental territory, closer to Jim O'Rourke's ambient side than to Pavement.

label: Mac's Record Label
description: Mac DeMarco's sixth solo album returns to his slack, chorus-drenched pop songwriting after the instrumental detour of Five Easy Hot Dogs, foregrounding sun-warped guitar tone and his familiar half-mumbled melodies. It is unhurried, private-sounding pop built for headphones on a walk. Fans of Salad Days will find the same loose, wobbly charm.
lineage: A return to the vocal jangle-pop songwriting of Salad Days and This Old Dog after an instrumental record, still rooted in his Captured Tracks-era slacker sound.

label: Ivy League Records
description: The Melbourne trio's debut EP sets out the template their albums would follow: three guitarists trading tightly interlocked jangling lines over driving, motorik rhythms. Five songs of unpretentious, sun-bleached guitar pop that announced the band before Hope Downs.
lineage: Grows out of the Go-Betweens/Triffids strand of Australian jangle-pop filtered through a more driving, Feelies-like guitar interplay.

label: Ivy League Records / Sub Pop
description: Their breakout EP, picked up by Sub Pop for US release, sharpens the interlocking three-guitar jangle of Talk Tight into tighter, more anthemic songs. It is the record that took the band from Melbourne club shows to international festival stages ahead of Hope Downs.
lineage: Bridges Talk Tight's homemade jangle-pop and the fuller, driving sound of Hope Downs, with the Feelies' interlocking-guitar template audible throughout.

label: Salinas Records
description: Sam Cook-Parrott's project piles sixteen scrappy, hook-heavy songs into under forty minutes, including a cover of Martha's 'Sycamore' and tributes to the band. It keeps the fuzzy, cassette-born intimacy of Something Wild and Torch Song while widening the emotional range.
lineage: Continues the Radiator Hospital/Swearin'/Waxahatchee axis of DIY Philadelphia guitar-pop that runs back through Sam Cook-Parrott's own Salinas Records scene.

label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
description: The Melbourne art-punk quartet's second album keeps the terse, sing-song melodies and four-way vocal trades of their debut, adding synths and violin to its punchy guitar songs. It is wry, hooky punk with a jangling underside, closer to Swell Maps than to hardcore.
lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY scene around Total Control/UV Race members, extending Terry HQ's terse punk-pop into slightly more orchestrated territory.

label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
description: Terry's third LP in three years keeps their formula of terrace-chant choruses and terse, witty verses, alternating scrappy Wire-like guitar scrambles with gentler, synth-shimmered passages. Its lyrics turn a sharper eye on nationalism and colonial history than the earlier records.
lineage: A continuation of the Melbourne post-punk/pop songwriting of Total Control and UV Race's overlapping membership, staying close to Terry HQ's terse jangle-punk template.

label: Upset the Rhythm / Anti Fade
description: Five years on from I'm Terry, the band's fourth album adds their most elaborate horn, string and piano arrangements yet to their terse four-vocal punk-pop, while lyrically taking aim at Australia's colonial history. It is the same detuned Fuzz Factory guitar tone with fuller production around it.
lineage: A late-period expansion of the same Melbourne art-punk lineage (Total Control, UV Race, Constant Mongrel side projects) that produced Terry HQ.

label: Winspear
description: Grand Rapids trio Major Murphy follows Access with eight songs that add strings for the first time, weaving classic-rock and vintage soft-rock touches into their usual blend of 1990s indie looseness and 1970s AM-radio warmth. It's their most psychedelic and emotionally direct record about parenthood and creative life.
lineage: Extends Major Murphy's own hybrid of 1990s indie rock and 1970s soft-rock songwriting established on Access, in the lineage of Big Star's more orchestrated moments.

label: Good Cheer Records
description: Mo Troper's scrappy, hook-crammed debut packs thirteen songs of GBV-scaled power pop into a lo-fi thirty minutes, full of pop-culture non-sequiturs (Judy Garland, Star Wars) delivered with a snotty, deadpan sneer. Pitchfork called its attitude 'snot-nosed pwnage,' which is the point.
lineage: Sits squarely in the Guided by Voices/Beulah four-track power-pop tradition that runs into the 2010s Portland DIY scene.

label: Good Cheer Records
description: Troper's fifteen-song second album sharpens Beloved's melodic instincts into a decade-end favorite for some critics, trading some of the lo-fi scrappiness for slightly cleaner hooks while keeping the rapid-fire, hyper-referential songwriting intact. It rarely lets a song run past two minutes.
lineage: Continues the GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting of Beloved, tightening the hooks in a way that anticipates Natural Beauty's more melodic turn.
key_tracks: Rock And Roll Will Change The World

label: Tender Loving Empire
description: Recorded after failed stints in LA and New York, Troper's third album swaps the earlier records' snottiness for plainer, more durable storytelling, anchored by the Kinks-indebted 'Jas From Australia' about a teenage internet romance. NPR called it 'grinningly great power-pop.'
lineage: A more melodically direct turn from Troper's earlier GBV-style scrappiness, closer to the Kinks and Teenage Fanclub end of the power-pop lineage.

label: K Records / Perennial
description: A sprawling twenty-one-song set from Kai Slater, packed with 1965-styled jangle hooks and endorsed on its sleeve by Robyn Hitchcock. It is the most maximalist Sharp Pins record yet, stringing together short, hook-forward pop songs with barely a pause between them.
lineage: Extends Sharp Pins' Nuggets/Big Star-derived jangle-pop into a longer, more song-crammed format, continuing the K Records/Perennial power-pop lineage.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: Nate Amos (also of Water From Your Eyes) re-recorded ten songs pulled from nine different releases in his sprawling This Is Lorelei back catalog, tracked quickly in a closet-sized Bed-Stuy room to keep the straight-to-Bandcamp spirit of the originals. It works as a breezy, guitar-pop-facing entry point to his catalog rather than a best-of.
lineage: A deliberate reconnection to Amos's earlier lo-fi Bandcamp songwriting after the breakout success of Box for Buddy, Box for Star.

label: Self-released
description: The Indianapolis band's follow-up to Triple Seven, a twelve-song set continuing their blend of fuzzy shoegaze guitar textures with unabashedly sweet, jangling pop melodies. It keeps the same sugar-and-noise balance that made Triple Seven a breakout.
lineage: Continues Wishy's fusion of shoegaze guitar-wall production with 1990s power-pop songwriting established on Triple Seven.

label: Damnably
description: Self-recorded and self-produced during lockdown at the Busan band's own studio, this is Say Sue Me's most inward record, built around themes of self-love and realization rather than the surf-jangle bounce of earlier singles. Guest spots from Korean jazz musicians Kim Ildu and Kim Oki widen the palette without losing the band's pristine, throwback jangle-pop core.
lineage: Continues the Busan band's pristine, Alvvays-adjacent throwback indie-pop songwriting, turning inward after Where We Were Together's touring cycle.

label: Merge Records
description: The London 'Celtic jangle boyband' moves to Merge for its third album, adding fiddle player Chris Haigh to push its shimmering, virtuosic guitar-pop even further, with a second, steelier vocal presence arguing against Owen Williams's familiar persona across songs about grief and regret. It's the most ambitious Tubs record yet.
lineage: Builds directly on Dead Meat and Cotton Crown's jangle-pop songwriting, adding fiddle to deepen the band's Wales/Britain folk-jangle hybrid.

label: Slumberland Records
description: Molina strips away Dissed and Dismissed's hardcore-scaled guitar crunch for eight mostly-acoustic, Bee Gees- and Byrds-indebted miniatures, none longer than two minutes. It's a hardcore lifer distilling decades of pop songcraft into brief, gutting fragments.
lineage: A quieter turn from the Weezer/Teenage Fanclub power-pop of Dissed and Dismissed toward the acoustic Big Star and Byrds side of the same lineage.

label: Slumberland Records
description: Molina brings full-band arrangements back after Confront the Truth's acoustic minimalism, opening with a twelve-string tune that could sit on a Byrds record and closing with gentle, Elliott Smith-like fingerpicking. Ten songs, none padded, all melody.
lineage: Splits the difference between Dissed and Dismissed's full-band crunch and Confront the Truth's acoustic intimacy, still working the Byrds/Big Star power-pop seam.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: Peter Gill's 24-song debut as 2nd Grade crams hook after hook into a scrappy, GBV-scaled power-pop sprawl, rarely settling into one idea for more than two minutes. It set the template for the project's compulsively prolific, miniature-song aesthetic.
lineage: A direct descendant of Guided by Voices' song-fragment power pop, part of the same Philadelphia scene as Hurry and Golden Apples.

label: Double Double Whammy
description: 2nd Grade's third full-length is its most expansive yet at 23 tracks, still built from the same rapid-fire jangling hooks and wry titles ('Jingle Jangle Nuclear Meltdown') as its predecessors. It is Peter Gill's project at its most prolific and melodically confident.
lineage: The latest entry in 2nd Grade's ongoing GBV/Big Star-indebted power-pop project, part of Philadelphia's mid-2020s jangle-pop scene.

label: Winspear
description: Slow Pulp's debut full-length was finished amid health crises and a pandemic, blending blown-out shoegaze guitar with unusually direct, hooky songwriting. It carries the explosive live intensity Terry first saw in Madison into a more controlled studio record.
lineage: Grows out of Slow Pulp's Chicago/Madison shoegaze-pop beginnings, a lighter, poppier cousin to Wednesday's countrygaze template.

label: ANTI-
description: Recorded at an internet-less cabin where a Lucinda Williams CD set the tone, Slow Pulp's second album warms its shoegaze-scale guitars with Americana hues and pristine pop hooks across ten filler-free tracks. It's their most confident synthesis of noise and twang.
lineage: Extends Moveys' shoegaze-pop into more overtly Americana-tinged territory, aligning with the countrygaze lineage of Wednesday and Great Grandpa.

label: ANTI-
description: Slow Pulp's third album, including a title track originally written during the Yard sessions, continues the band's move toward pristine, contemporary alt-rock that melds 1990s shoegaze scale with direct pop songwriting and higher emotional stakes.
lineage: A continuation of Yard's shoegaze-meets-Americana synthesis, pushing further into polished, radio-ready alt-rock.

label: Lame-O Records
description: Named for the euphoric first day of spring, Superviolet's debut is buoyant, hook-forward power pop written while its songwriter was falling in love and getting married. Ten unfussy, jangling songs that read as a career-best distillation of that songwriting style.
lineage: A Columbus, Ohio power-pop project in the Teenage Fanclub/Superchunk lineage, part of the same 2020s power-pop revival as Sharp Pins and Hurry.

label: Self-released
description: Lawn's second album, made 'with a sense of ease,' expands on the duo's breezy power-pop hooks across nine unhurried songs, with extra vocalists and keys filling out the sound ahead of the tighter Bigger Sprout. It's a warmer, more collaborative record than what came before or after.
lineage: Sits between Lawn's earlier, more post-punk-tinged material and the tighter power pop of Bigger Sprout and God Made The Highway.
